title: Products Of Binary Power Pieces
statement:
Write the positive number n as a sum of distinct powers of two (its binary digits) and list those powers in increasing order. Call that list pieces. For example, n = 13 gives pieces = [1, 4, 8].

Each query [l, r] asks for the product pieces[l] × pieces[l+1] × … × pieces[r]. Products get huge, so return each one modulo 1 000 000 007. Return the answers in query order.

examples.why: n = 2^29 − 1 has 29 pieces. The last two are 2^27 and 2^28; their product 2^55 overflows normal number precision, so it must be reduced modulo 1 000 000 007.

hints: The pieces are exactly the set bits of n, from the lowest bit up. How many can there be?
Every piece is a power of two, so a product of pieces is 2 raised to the sum of their exponents.

Store prefix sums of the exponents. Each query is then 2^(prefix[r+1] − prefix[l]) mod 1 000 000 007. The exponent never exceeds 0 + 1 + … + 29, so a small table of powers answers every query in O(1).

explain.intuition:
The binary digits of n are the only way to write it as distinct powers of two, so pieces is just its set bits, at most 30 of them. Multiplying powers of two adds exponents: 2^a × 2^b = 2^(a+b).

So turn each query into a sum of exponents, which a prefix-sum array answers instantly, and then into one power of two. The largest possible exponent is below 30 × 30 / 2, so precompute 2^e mod 1 000 000 007 for every e up to that bound by repeated doubling. Doubling a number below the modulus never leaves the safe integer range in JavaScript, unlike multiplying two large residues.
steps: Collect the exponents of the set bits of n from low to high: exps.
Build pow2[e] for e up to pre[last]: pow2[0] = 1, pow2[e] = 2 · pow2[e−1] mod M.
For each query [l, r], answer pow2[pre[r+1] − pre[l]].
pitfalls: Multiplying two residues near 10⁹ in JavaScript numbers. The product passes 2⁵³ and silently loses precision; use BigInt or the exponent trick.
Listing the pieces from the highest bit down. The order is increasing, so [0, 0] on n = 13 is 1, not 8.
Testing only small n. A missing modulo or an overflow only shows up when there are many pieces, like n = 2^29 − 1.

complexity.time: O(log n + q) after an O(log² n) power table

solutions.title: Multiply piece by piece with BigInt
solutions.idea: Build the pieces, then for each query multiply its pieces together modulo M. At most 30 multiplications per query.

solutions.title: Prefix sums of exponents + power table
solutions.idea: A product of powers of two is 2 to the sum of exponents. Prefix sums give the exponent; a precomputed table gives the power.

followups: Pieces are now an arbitrary array of numbers, not powers of two. How do you answer range products modulo a prime quickly?
Why does the prefix-product-and-divide trick need a modular inverse, and when can it fail?
